reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: FSGS is a pattern of podocyte injury rather than a single disease, defined by segmental scarring affecting only some (focal) glomeruli on light microscopy
Presents most often with nephrotic-range proteinuria, oedema and hypoalbuminaemia, though non-nephrotic proteinuria and microscopic haematuria also occur

A practical framework separates primary (podocytopathy, presumed circulating permeability factor), genetic (podocyte and slit-diaphragm gene mutations), secondary/adaptive (hyperfiltration, obesity, reduced nephron mass) and virus/drug-associated forms
APOL1 high-risk genotypes markedly increase risk in people of West African ancestry and influence prognosis and treatment response

Immunofluorescence is usually negative or shows non-specific segmental IgM and C3 trapping in sclerotic areas; electron microscopy shows diffuse foot-process effacement in primary disease and more segmental effacement in adaptive forms
Columbia (tip, cellular, collapsing, perihilar, not-otherwise-specified) histological variants carry differing prognostic and mechanistic implications

Immunosuppression/corticosteroids are directed at primary podocytopathy, whereas adaptive/secondary forms are managed with renin-angiotensin blockade and treatment of the underlying driver rather than immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: FSGS represents a common end pathway of injury to the visceral epithelial cell (podocyte). In primary disease a circulating permeability factor is thought to injure podocytes directly, producing widespread foot-process effacement and heavy proteinuria; genetic forms arise from mutations in podocyte cytoskeletal and slit-diaphragm proteins. Adaptive (secondary) FSGS follows glomerular hyperfiltration and increased capillary wall stress from reduced nephron mass, obesity or reflux, causing more limited effacement. Progressive podocyte depletion leaves denuded segments of glomerular basement membrane that adhere to Bowman's capsule and undergo segmental sclerosis, which spreads to involve more glomeruli and drives progressive renal impairment.
additionalDifferentials: IgA nephropathy with secondary segmental sclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to confirm the segmental sclerosis pattern and variant
Quantification of proteinuria by urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Serum albumin and lipid profile to characterise the nephrotic state
APOL1 genotyping and, in young or familial cases, a podocyte gene panel
Serologies and virology to exclude secondary and virus-associated causes (including HIV where relevant)
Renal imaging and assessment of nephron mass or obesity to identify an adaptive cause
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine with heavy proteinuria suggesting a collapsing or aggressive course
Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca, pleural effusions or thromboembolic complications
Acute kidney injury complicating the nephrotic state
Signs of an underlying secondary trigger such as advanced obesity, reflux nephropathy or viral infection
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying form and, critically, on the degree of proteinuria and its response to therapy. Patients achieving remission of nephrotic-range proteinuria have favourable long-term kidney survival, whereas persistent heavy proteinuria, the collapsing variant and APOL1 high-risk genotypes predict progression to end-stage kidney disease, and primary FSGS may recur after transplantation.
pitfalls: Labelling all FSGS as primary and giving prolonged immunosuppression when an adaptive or genetic cause is present
Missing focal lesions on an inadequate biopsy, since only some glomeruli are affected
Overlooking APOL1 risk and genetic testing in young or ancestry-relevant patients
Failing to distinguish collapsing glomerulopathy, which behaves far more aggressively
Attributing secondary sclerosis (from another glomerular disease) to primary FSGS
management: Treat primary (podocytopathic) disease with a prolonged course of corticosteroids as first-line immunosuppression, escalating to a calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus or ciclosporin for steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent disease
For adaptive/secondary FSGS, avoid immunosuppression and instead target the driver of hyperfiltration, notably weight reduction in obesity-related disease

Institute antiproteinuric and renoprotective therapy with renin-angiotensin system blockade (an ACE inhibitor or ARB) and dietary sodium restriction, adding an SGLT2 inhibitor for residual proteinuria
Support the nephrotic state with loop diuretics for oedema, statin therapy for hyperlipidaemia, and thromboprophylaxis given the hypercoagulability of heavy proteinuria
Monitor proteinuria response, renal function and drug toxicity, since remission of proteinuria is the key determinant of long-term kidney survival
Genotype-guided counselling — APOL1 high-risk and podocyte-gene forms respond poorly to immunosuppression, so recognise these to avoid futile treatment and to inform family screening
Refer to nephrology for biopsy-directed therapy and transplant planning, anticipating post-transplant recurrence of primary disease that may warrant plasma exchange and rituximab
